title: Chemical Bonding
tagline: Why atoms join, how electrons are shared or transferred, and what the bond type predicts about the compound.

overview.intro: Atoms bond because a joined arrangement has lower energy than separated atoms. This chapter works through the three ideas the syllabus asks for: the octet rule that explains when transfer happens, the sharing that builds covalent molecules, and the coordinate bond in which both electrons come from one partner. Each bond type is tied straight to properties, because the examination rarely asks for a definition alone; it asks why sodium chloride is a hard high-melting solid while hydrogen chloride is a gas.

facts.label: Octet rule
facts.value: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to reach a stable octet, like a noble gas.

facts.label: Electrovalency
facts.value: Number of electrons lost or gained in forming an ionic bond.

facts.label: Covalency
facts.value: Number of electron pairs shared by an atom in a covalent bond.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Definitions plus a properties comparison drawn from ionic and covalent compounds.

learningOutcomes: State the octet rule and use it to show the formation of an ionic bond by electron transfer with a dot-and-cross account.
Explain covalent bonding as sharing of electron pairs and draw single, double and triple bonds between named atoms.
Describe a coordinate bond as sharing of a lone pair donated by one atom and give one example.
Predict the properties of a compound from its bond type, covering melting point, conductivity and solubility.
Explain how electronegativity difference decides whether a bond is ionic, polar covalent or non-polar covalent.

learn.title: The octet rule and ionic bonding

blocks.text: A chemical bond is an attraction that holds atoms together because the combined system is more stable than the separate atoms. The octet rule says that atoms tend to arrange their outer electrons like a noble gas, which usually means eight electrons in the outer shell, or two for hydrogen and helium. When an electropositive metal meets an electronegative non-metal, the simplest way to reach that arrangement is transfer: the metal hands over its valence electrons and becomes a cation, the non-metal receives them and becomes an anion, and the electrostatic attraction between the two ions is the ionic or electrovalent bond. Sodium and chlorine make the classic case: sodium loses one electron to become Na+, chlorine gains one to become Cl-, and both reach the neon and argon arrangements respectively.

items: Ionic bonding needs one partner with low ionisation energy and one with high electron affinity.
The bond is a mutual attraction between oppositely charged ions arranged in a crystal lattice, not a link between just two atoms.
Electrovalency equals the number of electrons transferred, so sodium has electrovalency 1 and calcium 2.
Formation of an ionic compound is exothermic overall because lattice energy is released when ions come together.
Write the transfer in two steps before combining them: Na → Na+ + e-, then 2Cl + 2e- → 2Cl-, which gives 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl overall.
Magnesium oxide follows the same pattern: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-, O + 2e- → O2-, so Mg + 1/2 O2 → MgO shows the two electrons transferred.

items.note: Na (2, 8, 1) loses one electron to Na+ (2, 8); Cl (2, 8, 7) gains one to Cl- (2, 8, 8); attraction forms the bond.
Mg (2, 8, 2) loses two electrons to Mg2+; O (2, 6) gains two to O2- (2, 8); both reach a stable arrangement.

items.meaning: Bond formed by complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another, giving oppositely charged ions.
Positively charged ion formed when a metal atom loses electrons.
Negatively charged ion formed when a non-metal atom gains electrons.
Regular three-dimensional arrangement of ions in an ionic crystal.

blocks.text: When two atoms that both hold their electrons strongly approach each other, neither can take electrons outright, so they share a pair instead. One shared pair is a single covalent bond, two pairs make a double bond and three pairs make a triple bond. Covalency is the number of pairs an atom shares. Hydrogen reaches a duet, and every other atom in these simple molecules reaches an octet. The shared pairs hold the nuclei together, but because the atoms differ in electronegativity the sharing is often unequal, which makes many covalent molecules polar even though the compound as a whole is neutral.

items: Hydrogen forms one bond, carbon four, nitrogen three, oxygen two and the halogens one, each to complete its octet.
A single bond such as H-Cl is one shared pair; a double bond such as O=O is two pairs; a triple bond such as N≡N is three pairs.
Covalent compounds exist as discrete molecules, so their melting and boiling points stay low because only weak forces between molecules must be overcome.
Bond polarity grows with the electronegativity difference: C-H is almost non-polar, while H-Cl is strongly polar.

items.note: Each chlorine contributes one electron to a shared pair, and both reach the argon arrangement.
Oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen and keeps two lone pairs, giving a bent molecule and a polar bond.
Three shared pairs triple-bond the atoms, which is why nitrogen is so unreactive at room temperature.

blocks.caption: Ionic and covalent compounds compared
rows: Conducts when molten or in water
Does not conduct; no free ions
Usually soluble in water, insoluble in organic solvents
Soft, waxy or gases at room temperature

learn.title: Coordinate bonding and the shapes it suggests

blocks.text: A coordinate or dative bond is a shared pair in which both electrons come from the same atom. The donor supplies a lone pair, the acceptor supplies an empty orbital, and once formed the bond is indistinguishable from any other single covalent bond. The syllabus asks for this idea because it explains ions such as ammonium and molecules such as ammonia-boron trifluoride adducts, and because it shows that sharing can begin from one side. After the bond forms, every atom in the product still counts the shared pair in its octet, which is why the ammonium ion carries a single positive charge even though nitrogen formally donated both electrons.

items: The donor atom must have a lone pair; the acceptor must have a vacant orbital or incomplete octet.
An arrow is often drawn from donor to acceptor to show the direction of the electron pair donation.
In NH4+ the three N-H bonds are ordinary covalent bonds and the fourth is coordinate in origin but identical afterwards.
Coordinate bonding explains adduct formation, for example BF3 accepting a lone pair from NH3.

items.note: NH3 donates its nitrogen lone pair to H+, giving NH4+ with four equivalent N-H bonds and a single positive charge.
Nitrogen in NH3 donates a lone pair to boron in BF3, which has only six electrons around it.

items.meaning: Covalent bond in which both shared electrons are supplied by one atom.
Pair of electrons not involved in bonding that belongs to one atom alone.
Empty electron orbital available on an acceptor atom to receive a shared pair.

learn.title: From bond type to physical properties

blocks.text: The examination reward in this chapter goes to students who connect structure to property. Ionic compounds form giant lattices, so melting one means breaking many strong electrostatic attractions, which explains high melting points, hardness and brittleness. The lattice only releases mobile ions when molten or dissolved in water, so conductivity appears in those states and not as a solid. Covalent molecules are held together inside by strong bonds but between molecules only by weak attractions, so they melt easily and are poor conductors because no charged particle is free to move. A metal is the third case: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, which is why metals conduct in the solid state.

items: High melting point plus conduction when molten means giant ionic or giant covalent structure.
Low melting point plus no conduction means simple molecular structure.
Conduction as a solid means metallic bonding with delocalised electrons.
Solubility follows the rule of thumb: polar dissolves polar, and ionic compounds dissolve in water where ions can be hydrated.

items.text: Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C and conducts only when molten
items.note: The lattice must be broken to free the ions; the solid has no mobile charge carrier.

items.text: Hydrogen chloride is a gas at room temperature
items.note: Separate HCl molecules are held only by weak dipole forces, so little energy is needed to separate them.

blocks.caption: Bond type against observed properties
rows: Covalent bonds inside, weak forces outside
Positive ions in a sea of electrons

blocks.text: The same sharing idea scales continuously. When two identical atoms share, the pair sits exactly midway and the bond is non-polar. As the atoms differ, the more electronegative one pulls the pair towards itself, creating a dipole with a partial negative end and a partial positive end. Push the difference far enough and the electron is no longer shared at all: it is transferred, and the bond becomes ionic. So ionic and covalent bonding are ends of one scale, and the electronegativity difference tells you where a particular bond sits. This is why C-H bonds in hydrocarbons behave as non-polar while the O-H bonds in water behave as strongly polar and give water its hydrogen bonding.

items: Difference near zero: non-polar covalent, as in Cl2 or the C-H bond.
Intermediate difference: polar covalent, as in H-Cl or H2O, with partial charges on the atoms.
Large difference, typically a metal with a non-metal: electron transfer and an ionic bond.
A polar bond makes a molecule polar only if the bond dipoles do not cancel out in its geometry.

items.note: Each C=O bond is polar, but the linear molecule cancels the dipoles, so the molecule as a whole is non-polar.
The bent shape means the two O-H dipoles reinforce, giving a strongly polar molecule.

items.meaning: Separation of positive and negative charge within a bond or molecule.
Covalent bond in which the shared pair is displaced towards the more electronegative atom.
Bond between identical atoms or atoms of near equal electronegativity, with the pair shared equally.

keyPoints: A bond forms because the joined arrangement has lower energy than the separate atoms.
The octet rule: atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach a stable outer shell of eight, or two for hydrogen.
Ionic bonding is electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal, giving ions held in a lattice by electrostatic attraction.
Covalent bonding is sharing of one or more electron pairs; single, double and triple bonds share one, two or three pairs.
A coordinate bond is a shared pair donated entirely by one atom, as in NH4+.
Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct only when molten or dissolved; covalent compounds do neither.
Electronegativity difference scales from non-polar covalent through polar covalent to ionic.
Metallic bonding is positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, which is why metals conduct as solids.
Electrovalency counts electrons transferred; covalency counts electron pairs shared.
Polarity of a molecule depends on both bond polarity and molecular shape: dipoles can cancel.
examFocus: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams with every electron shown and label the octet that each atom achieves; unlabelled diagrams lose marks.
The ionic versus covalent properties table is a recurring question: learn at least four contrasting rows with named examples.
Define coordinate bonding in one sentence and give ammonium as the standard example with the direction of donation.
When asked why a compound has a property, name the structure first, then the forces, then the observation.

vocabulary.meaning: Tendency of atoms to acquire eight electrons in the outer shell.
Number of electrons an atom transfers to form an ionic bond.
Number of electron pairs an atom shares in covalent bonding.
Another name for a coordinate bond, where both shared electrons come from one atom.
Energy released when gaseous ions assemble into an ionic crystal.
A pair of equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance.
Metallic electrons not attached to any one atom and free to move through the lattice.
Unequal sharing of electrons in a bond, giving partial positive and negative ends.

questions.prompt: An ionic bond is formed by:
options: Transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal
Sharing of one lone pair only
questions.answer: Transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal
questions.explanation: Electron transfer creates oppositely charged ions, and their electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond.

questions.prompt: Which compound would be expected to have a high melting point and conduct electricity when molten?
questions.explanation: Only the ionic lattice has strong electrostatic forces between ions and releases mobile ions when molten.

questions.prompt: In a coordinate bond, the shared pair of electrons is supplied by:
options: One atom as a lone pair
questions.answer: One atom as a lone pair
questions.explanation: The donor donates a complete lone pair while the acceptor contributes an empty orbital.

questions.prompt: A molecule has polar bonds but no overall dipole. The reason is that:
options: The molecular shape makes the bond dipoles cancel
The atoms have equal atomic numbers
No lone pairs exist on any atom
questions.answer: The molecular shape makes the bond dipoles cancel
questions.explanation: Symmetrical geometry such as a linear O=C=O arrangement places equal and opposite dipoles that sum to zero.

questions.prompt: The number of electron pairs an atom shares in covalent bonding is called its __________.
questions.explanation: Covalency counts shared pairs, while electrovalency counts electrons transferred.

questions.prompt: The regular three-dimensional arrangement of ions in an ionic crystal is called a crystal __________.
questions.explanation: The lattice repeats the ion pattern in all directions and accounts for the crystal shape and brittleness.

questions.answer: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons so that their outer shell contains eight electrons, or two in the case of hydrogen and helium.
questions.explanation: A full outer shell corresponds to the stable electron arrangement of a noble gas.

questions.prompt: Explain why sodium chloride conducts electricity only when molten or dissolved in water.
questions.answer: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. In the solid lattice the ions are fixed in position, but melting or dissolving frees the Na+ and Cl- ions so they can move and carry charge.
questions.explanation: The ions exist in both states; only the freedom of movement differs.

questions.answer: A covalent bond in which both shared electrons are donated by one atom as a lone pair, while the other atom accepts the pair into an empty orbital.
questions.explanation: Once formed it is identical to an ordinary single covalent bond, but the origin of the pair differs.

questions.prompt: Compare the formation and properties of an ionic compound and a covalent compound.
questions.answer: In ionic bonding a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal, forming cations and anions held in a giant lattice by electrostatic attraction; the compound therefore has a high melting point, is hard but brittle, and conducts only when molten or dissolved because ions become free to move. In covalent bonding atoms share electron pairs to form discrete molecules; only weak forces act between molecules, so melting points are low, and with no charged particles present the substance does not conduct in any state. Solubility differs too: ionic compounds dissolve in water, covalent ones often dissolve in organic solvents.
questions.explanation: Structure determines properties: a giant lattice needs strong forces broken, discrete molecules do not, and conduction depends on mobile charge carriers.

questions.prompt: Draw a dot-and-cross account of the formation of magnesium chloride and explain why magnesium shows a valence of two.
questions.answer: Magnesium has the arrangement 2, 8, 2 and loses both valence electrons to reach the stable neon arrangement, becoming Mg2+. Each chlorine atom has 2, 8, 7 and gains one electron to reach the argon arrangement, becoming Cl-. Two chlorine atoms are therefore needed to accept the two electrons magnesium gives away, so the formula is MgCl2 and magnesium shows an electrovalency of two.
questions.explanation: The number of electrons magnesium must lose to reach a full shell fixes both its valence and the formula of its chloride.

questions.prompt: Explain why hydrogen chloride is a gas at 800 °C below the melting point of sodium chloride, even though both contain a polar bond.
questions.answer: Hydrogen chloride consists of separate HCl molecules; only weak dipole attractions act between molecules, so little energy separates them and the substance is already a gas at room temperature. Sodium chloride is a giant lattice in which every ion is held by strong electrostatic attraction to six neighbours, so a large amount of energy is needed to break the lattice, giving it a melting point of 801 °C. The polarity of an individual bond therefore says nothing about the melting point; the structure and the forces between particles decide it.
questions.explanation: Melting behaviour depends on what must be separated: molecules held by weak forces, or ions held in a lattice.
